query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled minor amount of Mo (e.g., 5–10 at.% substitution) to the TiVNbTa alloy will improve its high‐temperature strength by promoting an edge‐dislocation slip mode while maintaining its room‐temperature ductility and ensuring compatibility with W and CuCrZr heat-transfer requirements.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase BCC TiVNbTa alloy exhibiting ~800 MPa yield strength at room temperature (~40% strain) and reduced yield (∼330 MPa) and compressive strengths at 1273 K (∼423 MPa at 30% strain).
generation.intervention: Introduce a modest Mo content into the TiVNbTa alloy to form a quaternary high-entropy alloy; target composition adjustment ensuring about 5–10 at.% Mo replacing a portion of one of the base elements.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under high-temperature conditions (~1273 K) representative of divertor operation, while also confirming room-temperature ductility; the intermediate layer must remain thermally compatible with the adjacent W and CuCrZr components.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a homogeneous single-phase BCC microstructure with enhanced lattice distortion that favors a shift from screw-dominated to edge-dislocation-dominated deformation at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Mo, a high-melting point element, increases solid-solution strengthening and induces additional lattice distortions that lower the activation energy for edge dislocation motion. This promotes a slip mode transition at high temperatures, resulting in a plateau or improvement in yield strength without significantly compromising the ductile behavior at lower temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in high-temperature yield strength—potentially raising it from ~330 MPa to closer to 400–450 MPa—should be observed while maintaining similar ductility (∼40% strain) at room temperature. Thermal conductivity should not be significantly impaired, preserving effective heat transfer between W and CuCrZr.
generation.baseline: Reported performance of TiVNbTa with ~330 MPa yield strength at 1273 K and ~800 MPa at room temperature with 40% strain ductility.
generation.boundary: The enhancement must occur within the operating temperature ranges of both W (very high melting point) and CuCrZr (narrow operating window), ensuring that any modification does not compromise the efficient heat transfer or lead to phase instability or excessive brittleness.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Mo content for balancing high-temperature strength with room-temperature ductility and preserving thermal conductivity is not precisely known. There is also uncertainty about potential unintended effects on phase stability or heat transfer at the interfaces.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of TiVNbTa alloys with incremental Mo additions (e.g., 0%, 5%, and 10% at. substitution) using identical processing and homogenization treatments. Characterize the microstructure (XRD, TEM) to confirm single-phase BCC structures and assess dislocation mechanisms. Conduct mechanical testing at room temperature and 1273 K to measure yield strength, compressive strength, and ductility. Additionally, measure thermal conductivity to ensure compatibility with W and CuCrZr requirements.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength and ductility (strain to failure)
Microstructural analysis (phase identification, dislocation type via TEM)
Thermal conductivity across the operating temperature range
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Mo does not produce at least a 20% improvement in high-temperature yield strength compared to the baseline TiVNbTa alloy or if it leads to a significant reduction in room-temperature ductility or detrimental changes in thermal conductivity, then the hypothesis that Mo-induced lattice distortion enhances the high-temperature edge dislocation mechanism is falsified.

Enhanced Strength of a Mechanical Alloyed NbMoTaWVTi Refractory High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractA NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles.Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Edge-dislocation-induced ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength of HfMoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures.
